Prevention: Plant disease free and healthy planting materials.
Avoid planting cassava near alternate hosts such as pawpaw, guava and ornamental plants or remove them from near the cassava crop.
Plant early at the onset of rains.
Keep the field free from weeds and debris because they can be the source of infestation.
Cassava can be intercropped with legumes.
Bury or burn the infested plants after harvesting because flies can survive on crop residues and fly over long distances.
Monitoring: Scout by shaking the cassava to induce flying of the whiteflies.
They normally quickly fly in a circular manner and resettle after flying.
Look for whiteflies on the underside of the leaves.
They are generally active during the calm, still times of the day.
Look under the leaves for spiral patterns resembling fine cotton wool containing very tiny eggs and immature stages (nymphs).
Look for black sooty mould growing on the sugary secretions (sticky honeydew) that the whiteflies and their nymphs produce.
Control should be effected if flies population are seen on four or more cassava plants.
Direct Control: Use naturally occurring biological control agents such as
Encarsia spp., ladybird beetles and other parasitic wasps to control nymphal stages.
Remove affected plant parts and burn or bury more than 50cm deep.
Use soap ("alata soap") solution and water to spray the affected plants at a rate of 5-8g/litre of water.
Spray early in the morning or late afternoon.
Repeat application every 2 weeks if the problem persists.
Restrictions: Controlling the pest using insecticides is not recommended because pests may develop resistance to pesticides and destroy natural enemies.
